units.text: In the UAE, semaglutide is registered with the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) as Ozempic (injection, since 21 Oct 2019), Rybelsus (tablets, 31 Aug 2020) and Wegovy (FlexTouch injection, 14 Nov 2022; tablets, 4 May 2026); every entry checked is a Prescription Only Medicine (EDE register, 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, the EDE announced on 1 June 2026 that it had approved oral Wegovy (semaglutide) for long-term weight management in adults with obesity, or overweight with weight-related conditions, the second country to do so.

In the UAE, tirzepatide is registered as Mounjaro (injection, since 18 May 2022; KwikPen, 18 Jan 2024) as a Prescription Only Medicine; no product named Zepbound was found in the EDE register (25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, a MOHAP counterfeit alert on Mounjaro (Circular 9217/2024, relayed by DHA on 21 Oct 2024) described the genuine product as registered, with the indication 'treatment for type 2 diabetes mellitus and weight management'.
In the UAE, no registered product containing afamelanotide, and none named Scenesse, was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing tesamorelin, and none named Egrifta, was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing sermorelin was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing ipamorelin was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product matching 'CJC' or 'CJC-1295' was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing ibutamoren or named MK-677 was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing BPC-157 (searched as 'BPC-157', 'BPC 157' and 'pentadecapeptide') was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product matching 'TB-500', 'TB500' or 'thymosin' was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing KPV was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing LL-37 or cathelicidin was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product containing thymulin was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, no registered product matching 'PTD-DBM', 'PTD' or 'DBM' was found in the EDE register (ingredient and product-name search, 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, no registered medical product matching 'GHK', 'prezatide', 'copper tripeptide' or 'copper peptide' was found in the EDE register (25 Sep 2026); the register does not cover ordinary cosmetics, so copper-peptide cosmetics were not checked.

In Abu Dhabi, the Department of Health (Circular 112/2025, 2 July 2025), relaying an EDE warning on Melanotan II ('Barbie drug'), requires facilities to prohibit its importation, distribution, marketing or use; no melanotan product was found in the EDE register (25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, baricitinib is registered as Olumiant 2 mg and 4 mg tablets (since 8 Jun 2017), Prescription Only; the register files it under rheumatic diseases and does not show whether alopecia areata is an approved UAE indication.
In the UAE, topical minoxidil is registered (17 active entries, e.g. Regaine 5% solution since 28 Apr 1997, a Pharmacist Only Medicine; EDE register, 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, oral finasteride is registered, e.g. Propecia 1 mg (since 14 Jan 2003) and Proscar 5 mg (since 25 Mar 1993), with generics; Propecia is a Prescription Only Medicine (EDE register, 25 Sep 2026).
In the UAE, a topical finasteride spray, Fincrezo 2.275 mg/ml, has been registered since 24 Mar 2025 as a Prescription Only Medicine (EDE register, 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, somatropin is registered as Genotropin (since 13 Sep 2017), Norditropin FlexPro (10 Oct 2004), Omnitrope (4 May 2014) and Saizen (30 Jun 2013), and every somatropin entry is dispensed as a Semi Controlled Drug (SCD) (EDE register, 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, somatropin is on the federal list of semi-controlled medical products (MOHAP Ministerial Decision 306/2023, signed 24 Oct 2023), alongside the anabolic steroids mesterolone, parenteral nandrolone, stanozolol and oral or parenteral testosterone.

In the UAE, estradiol products for menopausal hormone therapy are registered as Prescription Only Medicines, e.g. Oestrogel 0.06% gel (since 11 Nov 2021) and Femoston tablets; the register gives therapeutic categories only, so whether any UAE label includes a skin indication was not verified (25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, oral collagen products are registered with the EDE as general-sale-list (GSL) health products rather than medicines, e.g. Collafix for Skin & Hair Health (bovine hydrolysed collagen, since 31 Aug 2023, pharmacy-only) and Centrum Skin, Hair & Nails (since 28 Apr 2025, general sale).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE; 'UAE Drug Corporation' in the official English translation) has been the federal authority regulating medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023 (issued 25 Sep 2023, in force 30 Sep 2023), with the power to approve and register medical products.

In the UAE, since 2 January 2025 (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, which replaced Federal Law 8/2019), no medical product may be imported, distributed, possessed, sold, displayed, used or manufactured for circulation without an EDE marketing approval.

In the UAE, physicians may prescribe a medicine for uses not in its leaflet, or a medicine never submitted for marketing approval, only when necessary, when no equivalent alternative is available and with the patient's approval; compassionate use is excluded from this rule (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 42(1)).

In Dubai, the DHA prohibits circulating, prescribing, dispensing, administering or using any peptide product unless it is registered or licensed with the EDE and used within the scope of its licence, and requires registered peptide products to be used strictly within their approved indications (External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).
In the UAE, medical products compounded in licensed compounding pharmacies are exempt from the marketing-approval requirement (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 5(2), in force 2 Jan 2025).

In the UAE, a compounding pharmacy may not compound essential copies of products holding an EDE marketing approval unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient, and may not formulate products intended for research, development or experimentation (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 95).

In Abu Dhabi, the DoH Standard for Provision of Compounding Pharmacy Services (August 2026) allows compounding only for a genuine, documented clinical need that no suitable licensed product meets, and bars copying commercially available products for convenience or cost or introducing experimental or unverified products.

In Abu Dhabi, compounding requires a Good Compounding Practice (GCP) certificate issued by the EDE, and compounding from unapproved or unknown-source substances, or from substances not on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances, is prohibited unless the DoH permits it (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

In Abu Dhabi, the DoH treats peptides as emerging, non-monographed, high-risk substances: novel substances of unknown risk may be compounded only if monographed, a component of an approved medicine, or listed on the DoH Registry for Compounded Substances (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

In Abu Dhabi, where emerging substances such as peptides are permitted, prescribing is limited to eligible facilities and credentialed prescribers for accepted indications, office-stock ordering to hospitals and DoH-approved specialty clinics, and compounding pharmacies must dispense only against individual prescriptions (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

In Abu Dhabi, compounded peptide formulations may use only certified active ingredients imported under EDE oversight, clinics must hold technical agreements with licensed compounding pharmacies, and peptide products must be traceable from source to patient (DoH Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

In Dubai, the DHA prohibits using any peptide product intended for research use on humans or for therapeutic purposes outside a study or clinical trial approved by the competent authority (External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

In Dubai, facilities may not buy, accept or use peptide products from websites, social media, individual accounts or unlicensed or unverifiable suppliers, and products without full identification data (active substance, concentration, batch, expiry) may not be used (DHA External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).
In the UAE, Federal Decree-Law 38/2024 brings cosmetics with a medical effect on the skin, hair or nails within its definition of medical products regulated by the EDE.

In the UAE, the EDE registers 'healthcare products' not intended to diagnose, treat or prevent disease, including dietary supplements, herbal products and cosmetics with a medical effect, through a marketing authorisation valid for five years (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, whether a borderline product (for example a peptide serum) needs an EDE marketing authorisation, and in which category, is settled by an EDE classification letter based on the product's presentation, composition, use and design (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

In the UAE, ordinary cosmetics and personal-care products are a MoIAT-regulated product category under Cabinet Resolution 18/2014 (the UAE control system for cosmetics and personal care products), needing a conformity certificate backed by accredited test reports, a formula declaration and a product safety report.

In Abu Dhabi, the DoH classes topical cosmetic peptides with no systemic effect as low-risk products that stay under existing regulatory pathways, while systemic, regenerative or weakly evidenced peptides face enhanced controls (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).
In the UAE, food supplements are medical products under Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, defined as oral products that support the diet and do not treat, diagnose or prevent disease.

In the UAE, advertising or promoting any medical product by any means, including social media, requires EDE approval, and advertising controlled or semi-controlled products to the public is prohibited (Federal Decree-Law 38/2024, Art. 44).

In the UAE, an EDE licence to advertise a medical product requires a valid EDE marketing authorisation for the product (only products exempted by the Cabinet under Art. 5(3) of Federal Decree-Law 38/2024 are excused), a licensed pharmaceutical or healthcare establishment as applicant, and truthful, evidence-based content matching the approved indications (EDE service page, read 25 Sep 2026).

In Dubai, the DHA bans misleading or unproven peptide claims, including anti-aging, cell regeneration, weight loss, muscle building and improved appearance, unless the use is within the product's approved status, and requires any promotion of unregistered materials, including through influencers or social media, to stop (29 July 2026).

In Abu Dhabi, healthcare providers may not promote peptide therapies with misleading or unsubstantiated claims, or advertise, market or publish media content about them without prior approval from the DoH and relevant authorities (Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

In Abu Dhabi, emerging and non-monographed compounded substances such as peptides may not be advertised, promoted or marketed, directly or indirectly, to patients or healthcare professionals (DoH compounding standard, August 2026).

In Dubai, peptide products may be prescribed, dispensed or administered only by licensed, authorised professionals in a licensed facility, and injections or IV therapies for 'wellness', 'recovery', 'detoxification' or 'energy enhancement' are not permitted without a documented medical indication and treatment plan (DHA External Circular 0867, 29 July 2026).

In Abu Dhabi, physicians may prescribe peptide therapies only for clinical indications supported by available scientific evidence, after a documented eligibility assessment and with informed consent that covers benefits, uncertainties, risks, alternatives and the product's regulatory approval status (DoH Circular 148/2026, 31 July 2026).

In the UAE, the EDE warned on 20 Jul 2026 (Circular 31/2026) that 1,659 packs of Mounjaro and Ozempic stolen from a German wholesaler are outside the legitimate supply chain, and told the public to buy these medicines only from licensed pharmacies.
In Dubai, the DHA sent MOHAP Circular 06 of 2025 on the serious safety concerns of Melanotan II ('Barbie drug') to all private health facilities for adherence (25 Jun 2025).

In Brazil, Ozempic (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk) has been registered by ANVISA since 6 Aug 2018; its label (Sep 2026 check) indicates it only for adults with inadequately controlled type 2 diabetes, including kidney-outcome risk reduction in type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease.

In Brazil, Wegovy (semaglutide, Novo Nordisk) has been registered by ANVISA since 2 Jan 2023 for chronic weight management in adults (BMI ≥30, or ≥27 with a weight-related comorbidity) and in adolescents aged 12 or over with obesity and body weight above 60 kg.

In Brazil, the semaglutide patent expired on 20 Mar 2026 and ANVISA registered the first synthetic semaglutide pen (Ozivy, EMS) on 26 May 2026, followed by five more synthetic pens on 29 Jul 2026; these copies are indicated for type 2 diabetes, not weight management. ANVISA's register listed 15 active semaglutide products on 25 Sep 2026.

In Brazil, Mounjaro (tirzepatide, Eli Lilly) has been registered by ANVISA since 25 Sep 2023; its label covers type 2 diabetes, chronic weight management in adults and obstructive sleep apnoea. No product named Zepbound was found in ANVISA's register (25 Sep 2026).

In Brazil, no registered medicine containing afamelanotide (Scenesse) was found: ANVISA's open-data register and its online medicines search returned no match on 25 Sep 2026, and the substance is absent from ANVISA's substance dictionary.

In Brazil, no registered medicine containing melanotan was found in ANVISA's register (25 Sep 2026); no ANVISA resolution naming melanotan was found in the Diário Oficial search, so unregistered-medicine rules apply rather than a specific ban.

In Brazil, Olumiant (baricitinib, Eli Lilly) has been registered by ANVISA since 26 Nov 2018; its current label includes severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 or over weighing at least 30 kg, besides rheumatoid arthritis, atopic dermatitis and COVID-19.

In Brazil, minoxidil is registered as an anti-alopecia medicine (for example Aloxidil 5%, indicated for androgenetic alopecia in adult men); every active minoxidil registration sits in the anti-alopecia class, and the oral antihypertensive Loniten registrations are all inactive (register, 25 Sep 2026).

In Brazil, 1 mg finasteride products such as Pro Hair are registered for male-pattern hair loss in men and are not indicated for women or children; the Propecia brand registration is inactive (register, 25 Sep 2026).

In Brazil, somatropin is registered (for example Genotropin, Pfizer, registered 12 Aug 2019) for growth disorders in children and for replacement therapy in adults with severe growth hormone deficiency; skin or anti-ageing uses are not labelled indications.
In Brazil, somatropin is a controlled substance on List C5 (anabolic substances) of Portaria SVS/MS 344/1998, as updated by RDC 1.036/2026, and needs a special-control prescription in two copies.
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing tesamorelin (including Egrifta) was found in ANVISA's register or online search (25 Sep 2026).
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing sermorelin was found in ANVISA's register or online search (25 Sep 2026).
In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that injectable ipamorelin products are not registered in any category.
In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that CJC-1295 products are not registered in any category.
In Brazil, ibutamoren is not a registered medicine, and on 9 Jun 2026 ANVISA refused the clinical-trial petitions for ibutamoren mesylate (LUM-201) (RE 2.318/2026).
In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that BPC-157 is not registered as a medicine and is not authorised as a food supplement, and that no company has applied for supplement authorisation.
In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that TB-500 is not registered as a medicine and is not authorised as a food supplement.
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing KPV was found in ANVISA's register (25 Sep 2026).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that injectable GHK-Cu products are not registered and are illegal for any health or aesthetic use; topical GHK-Cu cosmetics are a separate category (see cosmetics).
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing LL-37 (cathelicidin) was found in ANVISA's register, and the substance is absent from ANVISA's substance dictionary (25 Sep 2026).

In Brazil, no registered medicine containing thymulin was found in ANVISA's register (25 Sep 2026); thymus-derived immunomodulators with other actives (thymomodulin, Leucogen; thymostimulin) do hold active registrations.
In Brazil, no registered medicine containing PTD-DBM was found in ANVISA's register (25 Sep 2026).
In Brazil, topical tretinoin (for example Vitacid, Theraskin) is registered, and its label names cutaneous photoageing as well as acne vulgaris, for dermatological use in adults and patients over 12.

In Brazil, estradiol for menopausal hormone therapy is registered (for example Oestrogel, Besins); the label read covers menopausal symptoms and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, and skin ageing is not a labelled indication.

In Brazil, oral collagen is regulated as a food supplement, not a medicine; ANVISA's Jan 2025 guidance lists an approved skin-health claim for 2 kDa bioactive collagen peptides, restricted to products meeting an ANVISA-set minimum content, for adults only.

In Brazil, a compounded (magistral) preparation must be made individually by the pharmacy against a prescription from an authorised professional that sets its composition, form and dosing (RDC 96/2008 definition).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that any substance must have undergone efficacy and safety assessment before it can be compounded, and that compounding may only be individual, on a medical prescription, by a compounding pharmacy licensed by local health surveillance.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated in Nov 2024 that compounded medicines should be used only when the registered industrial product is unavailable in the dose or dosage form the patient needs, and that only APIs with a current or past registration may be compounded into hormonal implants.

In Brazil, Nota Técnica 200/2025 (Aug 2025) allows compounding of GLP-1 agonists only in narrow conditions: synthetic APIs only if a registered medicine with the same molecule exists, biotech APIs only from the manufacturer assessed at registration, with mandatory quality testing; at that date synthetic semaglutide could not be imported or compounded.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated in Apr 2025 that its measure does not change the physician's right to prescribe medicines for purposes other than those on the label (off-label use), when the physician considers that, for a given patient, the benefits outweigh the risks.
In Brazil, no medicine, including an imported one, may be manufactured, sold or supplied before it is registered (Law 6.360/1976, art. 12).

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that some injectable peptides are not regularised in any category (food, medicine, cosmetic or supplement) and are therefore illegal for any health use, including aesthetic use.
In Brazil, ANVISA stated in Jul 2026 that an investigational (experimental) medicine is used exclusively in authorised clinical research.

In Brazil, unregistered medicines may be imported only exceptionally, for strictly personal use, with a medical prescription; when ANVISA publishes a specific prohibition (as for several GLP-1 pens in 2025–2026), import by any route is suspended.
In Brazil, ANVISA stated in Sep 2025 that use of an unregistered imported medicine is entirely the responsibility of the patient and the prescribing physician.

In Brazil, cosmetic labelling may not carry therapeutic claims for the product or its ingredients (RDC 907/2024, art. 12), so a peptide serum that claims to treat a condition falls outside the cosmetic category.

In Brazil, ANVISA stated on 2 Jul 2026 that injectable cosmetics do not exist; an injectable product offered as a cosmetic is irregular. Topical products named after GHK-Cu do appear as notified cosmetics in ANVISA's cosmetics dataset (221 entries, 25 Sep 2026); ANVISA cancelled several GHK-Cu cosmetic processes on 29 Apr 2026 without published reasons (RE 1.771/2026).
In Brazil, a food supplement is by definition a product for oral ingestion for healthy people (RDC 243/2018), so no injectable supplement can exist.
In Brazil, the constituents a food supplement may use are those on ANVISA's authorised list (IN 28/2018); constituents not on the list must not be used.

In Brazil, promotion of prescription-only medicines is restricted to media aimed exclusively at professionals who can prescribe or dispense them, and online promotion must sit behind a registration wall for those professionals (RDC 96/2008, arts 27 and 29).

In Brazil, compounding pharmacies may give only prescribers factual material naming active substances and referenced indications, with no brand names, prices or promotional content (RDC 96/2008, art. 36); ANVISA restated in Nov 2024 that advertising compounded products to the public is not permitted.

In Brazil, since 23 Jun 2025 all GLP-1 agonist medicines (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide, tirzepatide and others), industrial or compounded, need a two-copy prescription valid 90 days that the pharmacy retains (RDC 973/2025 and IN 360/2025).

In Brazil, the Federal Council of Medicine bars physicians from using anabolic steroids or androgens for aesthetic purposes or performance, and from prescribing hormones marketed as "bioidentical" or "nano" without proof of superiority (CFM Resolution 2.333/2023, in force since its publication on 11 Apr 2023; listed as in force on 25 Sep 2026).

In Brazil, CFM Resolution 1.999/2012 (in force Sep 2026) bars physicians from using hormones, including growth hormone, to prevent, delay, modulate or reverse ageing, except to replace a diagnosed deficiency with proven benefit.

In Brazil, CFM Resolution 2.336/2023 on medical advertising forbids physicians to promote medicines not registered with ANVISA or to take part in product advertising that implies guaranteed results; before-and-after images must show satisfactory and unsatisfactory outcomes and complications.

In Brazil, ANVISA inspections between Jan and Apr 2026 led to interdiction of 8 of the 26 compounding pharmacies and importers assessed and seized over 1.3 million irregular injectable units; ANVISA and the Federal Police issued a joint technical note on 6 May 2026 on crimes involving irregular GLP-1 medicines.
In the EU, semaglutide is a centrally authorised prescription medicine: Ozempic and Rybelsus for type 2 diabetes and Wegovy for weight management (EMA and HMA, June 2024).
In the EU, Ozempic (semaglutide) has held an EU-wide marketing authorisation since 8 February 2018 and is prescription-only (EMA).
In the EU, Wegovy (semaglutide) has held an EU-wide marketing authorisation for weight management since 6 January 2022 and is prescription-only (EMA).

In the EU, tirzepatide is authorised as Mounjaro (EU-wide authorisation 15 September 2022) for type 2 diabetes and adult weight management, prescription-only; no EU product named Zepbound was found in the Union Register or EMA data (searched 25 September 2026).

In the EU, afamelanotide (Scenesse implant) is authorised only for erythropoietic protoporphyria, under exceptional circumstances (European Commission, 22 December 2014), and is prescribed only by specialists in recognised EPP centres.

In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing melanotan (Melanotan II) was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).

In the EU, baricitinib (Olumiant) has been centrally authorised since 13 February 2017; its indications include severe alopecia areata in adults and adolescents aged 12 and over, and it is prescription-only, started by a doctor experienced in the condition (EMA).

Since EMA's January 2023 review, JAK inhibitors including Olumiant should be used in people aged 65 or over, at raised cardiovascular or cancer risk, or long-term smokers only if no suitable alternative exists, and this applies to alopecia areata.

In the EU, topical minoxidil medicines are authorised nationally (no centrally authorised product was found); after an EU safety review (CMDh, June 2024) their product information warns of reversible excess hair growth in infants after skin contact with a caregiver's application site.
In the EU, finasteride 1 mg tablets and a finasteride skin spray are authorised nationally in various member states for early androgenetic alopecia in men aged 18 to 41 (EMA, 2025).

After an EU-wide review endorsed by the CMDh on 19 June 2025, suicidal ideation is a confirmed side effect of finasteride tablets; people taking 1 mg for hair loss who notice mood changes should stop and seek advice, and packs carry a patient card.

In the EU, somatropin is an injectable medicine authorised since the 1980s through central and national procedures for growth hormone replacement and for short stature in specific childhood conditions (EMA, 2012).
In the EU, the centrally authorised somatropin Omnitrope (since 12 April 2006) is prescription-only, and treatment is started and monitored by a doctor experienced in growth disorders (EMA).

In the EU, tesamorelin has no marketing authorisation: the application for Egrifta (excess abdominal fat in HIV lipodystrophy) was withdrawn on 21 June 2012 when the CHMP's provisional view was that it could not be approved, partly because raised IGF-1 was a major safety concern.
In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing sermorelin was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).
In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing ipamorelin was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).
In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing CJC-1295 was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).

In the EU, ibutamoren (MK-677) is not an authorised medicine; it holds an orphan designation for growth hormone deficiency (EU/3/17/1882, 20 June 2017), which EMA states is not a marketing authorisation.
In the EU, no centrally authorised medicine containing BPC-157 was found in the Union Register or in EMA's data on authorised, refused and withdrawn medicines (searched 25 September 2026).

In the EU, tretinoin (retinoic acid) is banned in cosmetics (Annex II entry 375), and the Commission's borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product containing it that is marketed as a cosmetic is an illegal cosmetic (June 2025).

In the EU, the harmonised core product information for HRT products (CMDh, December 2025) lists oestrogen-deficiency symptoms after menopause, osteoporosis prevention and vaginal atrophy as indications — skin is not an indication.

In the EU, oestrogens and progestogens are prohibited in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II entries 260 and 194), so a hormone-containing 'cosmetic' skin cream is not lawful as a cosmetic.

In the EU, the Commission refused (Regulation (EU) No 1154/2014) a claim that a collagen peptide mixture maintains skin health by increasing elasticity and reducing wrinkles, because a cause-and-effect relationship was not established; the EU Register lists no authorised claim for collagen itself (searched 25 September 2026).

In the EU, medicines prepared in a pharmacy for an individual patient on prescription (magistral formula) or to a pharmacopoeia for the pharmacy's own patients (officinal formula) are outside Directive 2001/83/EC, so they need no marketing authorisation under it (Article 3).

EU law exempts pharmacists who prepare medicines solely for retail supply in dispensing pharmacies from the manufacturing authorisation that all other manufacture needs (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 40(2)).
In the EU, no medicine may be placed on a member state's market without a national marketing authorisation or an EU-wide (central) authorisation (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 6(1)).

EU law lets each member state, under its own legislation, allow an unauthorised medicine for an individual patient on a bona fide unsolicited order from an authorised health professional, under that professional's direct personal responsibility (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 5(1)).

EMA and HMA's shortage steering group asked EU prescribers in June 2024 to prescribe GLP-1 receptor agonists only for their authorised uses and said these medicines are not approved for, and should not be used for, cosmetic weight loss.

Under EU law a product is a medicine by presentation (presented as treating or preventing disease) or by function (restoring, correcting or modifying physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action), and where a product could be both a medicine and another regulated product, medicines law applies (Directive 2001/83/EC, Articles 1(2) and 2(2)).
The research exclusion in Directive 2001/83/EC concerns medicinal products intended for research and development trials and is without prejudice to EU clinical-trials law (Article 3(3)).

On 3 September 2025 EMA and HMA warned of a sharp rise in illegal medicines sold online and on social media as GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, tirzepatide); these products are unauthorised and may not contain the stated substance.
In the EU, anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted is not a cosmetic (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Article 2(2)), so an injected peptide can never be a cosmetic.

The EU borderline manual (version 5.4, November 2024, retained in 5.5) says a product in a vial or ampoule for injection cannot be a cosmetic, and one sold as a cosmetic must be clearly for external use and not marketed with a device allowing injection or delivery below the epidermis.

Whether an EU product is a cosmetic is decided case by case by national authorities; the borderline manual says an anti-wrinkle product that significantly restores, corrects or modifies physiological functions by a pharmacological, immunological or metabolic action does not qualify as a cosmetic (June 2025).

Before an EU cosmetic is placed on the market it needs a responsible person in the EU, a safety assessment with a cosmetic product safety report, and electronic notification to the Commission (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Articles 4, 10 and 13).

EU cosmetic claims must be supported by adequate and verifiable evidence, and a claim that extrapolates an ingredient's properties (for example a peptide's) to the finished product needs evidence such as the ingredient's presence at an effective concentration (Regulation (EU) No 655/2013).

In the EU, food supplements are foods that supplement the normal diet, are concentrated sources of nutrients or other substances with a nutritional or physiological effect, and are sold in measured doses such as capsules, tablets or sachets (Directive 2002/46/EC, Article 2(a)).
In the EU, a health claim on a food is prohibited unless it is authorised and included in the EU lists of authorised claims (Regulation (EC) No 1924/2006, Article 10(1)).
In the EU, food information, including advertising, must not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease (Regulation (EU) No 1169/2011, Article 7(3) and (4)).

EU law requires member states to prohibit any advertising of a medicine that has no marketing authorisation, and advertising of authorised medicines must match the summary of product characteristics (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 87).

EU law requires member states to prohibit advertising of prescription-only medicines to the general public (Directive 2001/83/EC, Article 88(1)(a)); 'advertising' includes any inducement designed to promote prescription, supply, sale or consumption (Article 86(1)).

EU audiovisual law bans audiovisual commercial communications for prescription-only medicines and medical treatment, and video-sharing platforms must take measures to apply this to advertising on their services, including advertising they do not sell themselves (Directive 2010/13/EU, Articles 9(1)(f) and 28b(2)).
