The skin works as a peripheral neuro-immuno-endocrine organ: reviews describe four immuno-endocrine units (epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal) whose cells make and respond to hormones and signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the circulation. This is a mechanistic framework drawn from cell, tissue and animal work.

Skin cells carry the enzymes to make steroids from cholesterol (CYP11A1) and to activate circulating precursors (11β-HSD1, 5α-reductase, aromatase), producing cortisol, DHT and estradiol locally; this rests mainly on cell, tissue and biochemical studies.

Human scalp hair follicles kept in organ culture respond to CRH by making POMC products, secrete cortisol, and switch off their own CRH in response to glucocorticoid — an HPA-like loop running without systemic connections (human tissue, ex vivo).

In mice, deleting glucocorticoid synthesis in keratinocytes causes spontaneous skin inflammation and worse experimental dermatitis: keratinocyte-made glucocorticoids set local immune tone (animal evidence, with a human association with inflammatory skin disease).

The skin also runs shortened thyroid-like (TRH, TSH, deiodinase-generated T3) and somatotropic (GH/IGF-1) loops; the thyroid-like evidence comes mainly from mouse models and the follicle GH/IGF-1 loop from human follicles ex vivo.

The skin supplies a whole-body hormone system: UVB converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to previtamin D3 in human skin, and vitamin D3 is carried into the circulation to be hydroxylated to 25(OH)D and then calcitriol (skin-to-body signalling).
Reviews describe a skin contribution to circulating androgens and estrogens, especially in older people — a second skin-to-body route, supported mainly by biochemical data.

Systemic hormones act on skin (body-to-skin): cortisol excess thins the dermis and causes striae and bruising; hypothyroidism gives dry, coarse skin and myxoedema. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen and lists suspected Cushing syndrome (violaceous striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, new hypertension or diabetes) and rapidly progressive virilisation among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology.

The Hormone Cell Atlas (Science 2026) analysed RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them, and mapped putative hormone-producing and hormone-receiving cell types.

The atlas's authors describe its scores as putative and hypothesis-generating, not functional hormones and receptors, and leave validation to in vitro and in vivo work; more generally, transcript levels alone often fail to predict protein levels. A transcriptomic map therefore shows capacity, not secretion or effect.

The guide infers from the atlas that the skin, built from every major cell lineage, is plausibly one of the body's largest distributed endocrine signalling networks — an inference from transcriptomic prediction, not a measurement.

Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and local steroid-metabolising enzymes modify potency, so the cutaneous response need not mirror the dose; receptor presence is a hypothesis-generating starting point that needs validation, and says nothing yet about efficacy in people.

The guide's testing pearl says serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D falls with sunscreen use; an independent systematic review found that sunscreen blocks vitamin D synthesis under artificial UV, but randomized field trials of daily moderate-SPF sunscreen did not lower 25(OH)D, and high-SPF products have not been trialled.

Senescent cells are permanently growth-arrested yet still secreting; the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (IL-6, IL-8, matrix metalloproteinases, growth factors) was characterised in cultured human cells after DNA damage.

In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a are more numerous with age in both epidermis and dermis; no single universal marker identifies senescent cells, so counts depend on the marker used.

In 178 adults of the Leiden Longevity Study, more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin were associated with ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and higher perceived age independent of chronological age; people in the lowest tertile of epidermal p16 counts looked about 3 years younger than those in the highest. This is an association, not evidence of cause.

Skin collagen falls with age; aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1, fragmented collagen and fibroblasts under less mechanical tension that make less procollagen, and culture work shows fragmentation feeds back to raise MMP-1. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible but not shown.

Causal evidence that senescent cells drive ageing comes from mice: clearing p16-positive cells extended healthy lifespan and senolytics improved function and survival in old mice; skin was checked only for safety (thickness, fibrosis, wound closure), and clearing p16-positive cells during healing slowed wound closure.

Human senotherapy data are small pilots with tissue-marker endpoints — an open-label senolytic pilot in 9 patients reduced epidermal p16/p21-positive cells; an exploratory topical rapamycin RCT (36 enrolled, 19 lost) reduced skin p16 — clinical improvement in that trial was described only in 'multiple participants', and no adequately sized trial with clinical skin-ageing outcomes was found on PubMed or ClinicalTrials.gov (checked 24 September 2026). The guide advises that senolytics generally be confined to clinical trials.

Interventions on the ageing matrix with human trials: daily sunscreen slowed photoageing in a 903-person community RCT (B); topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials and the guide rates topical retinoids first-line GRADE A; topical retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small RCT (C), and within a week lowered MMPs and raised collagen synthesis in aged human skin.

The skin expresses the elements of a local HPA-like axis (CRH, POMC, ACTH) and regenerates active cortisol from cortisone through 11β-HSD1 in keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts; 11β-HSD1 activity is higher in aged and photo-exposed human skin, local glucocorticoid availability is regulated independently of circulating levels, and 11β-HSD1 knockout mice are protected from age-induced dermal atrophy.

The only human RCT of 11β-HSD1 inhibition with skin outcomes is a 28-person pilot in type 2 diabetes: it missed its primary outcome (skin 11β-HSD1 activity), showed an exploratory reduction in wound size, and modestly impaired barrier function. No registered trial tests an 11β-HSD1 inhibitor for skin ageing, and the compound tested has no FDA approval (ClinicalTrials.gov and Drugs@FDA checked 24 Sep 2026).

Per the Endocrine Society diagnostic guideline, the features that best discriminate Cushing's syndrome are easy bruising, facial plethora, proximal myopathy and striae that are reddish-purple and wider than 1 cm; facial fullness, dorsocervical fat pad, weight gain, acne, hirsutism, thin skin and fatigue are common in the general population and less discriminatory.

Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon (2–3 new cases per million per year in European population studies); the commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, and the guideline recommends a drug history (oral, inhaled, topical, injected — including skin-bleaching creams, herbal tonics and joint or nerve injections) before any biochemical testing.

The guideline recommends testing patients with multiple and progressive features (particularly the discriminating ones) or features unusual for age, recommends against widespread testing and against random serum cortisol, and sends abnormal results to an endocrinologist. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide adds that consumer cortisol panels are poorly validated and reads most popular 'cortisol face' as a lifestyle-and-fluid picture.

Human skin expresses ERα, ERβ and GPR30 in aged and photoaged sites; two weeks of topical estradiol raised procollagen I/III in sun-protected hip skin of postmenopausal women but not in photoaged forearm or facial skin.

In small observational biopsy studies, skin collagen content and thickness fall by about 1–2% per year after menopause, in step with bone mass, tracking years since menopause more than chronological age. The 'up to 30% in the first five years' figure quoted by reviews and by the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide is not stated in the primary abstracts it traces to; the lesson reports it as a review figure.

Small RCTs of systemic hormone therapy increased skin thickness (n=60, 12 months) and skin collagen (n=41, 6 months) at non-facial sites; a 2023 meta-analysis pooling small, heterogeneous studies (some non-randomized) reports higher elasticity, thickness and collagen, and its authors do not propose MHT as an independent treatment for skin ageing.

The largest RCT of hormone therapy on facial skin (485 women, 48 weeks, low-dose) found no significant difference from placebo in wrinkling or sagging, and a 4-year randomized study in recently menopausal women (KEEPS) found no difference in wrinkle or rigidity scores. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the NAMS 2022 statement rates its skin key point Level II (limited or inconsistent); the course grades the structural effects C and states that a visible wrinkle benefit has not been shown in the largest trials.

Topical estrogen: a 24-week RCT (n=54) of a conjugated-estrogen cream improved facial skin thickness and fine wrinkles versus placebo cream, and a small randomized study found topical estrogen accelerated acute wound healing in healthy older adults. In the US an OTC product promoted as a hormone cream is regarded as an unapproved new drug (21 CFR 310.530), and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide advises against off-label estrogen for wrinkles (GRADE C).

In the US (FDA request of 10 Nov 2025; first approved labels 12 Feb 2026), approved uses of menopausal hormone therapy are moderate-to-severe vasomotor symptoms, vulvovaginal/genitourinary symptoms and, for some products, prevention of bone loss; the labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and probable-dementia statements from the boxed warning and did not add skin as an indication.

The NAMS 2022 position statement finds the benefit–risk ratio favourable for bothersome VMS and prevention of bone loss in women under 60 or within 10 years of menopause without contraindications, and finds insufficient evidence and safety concerns for compounded bioidentical hormone therapy (patient preference alone should not justify it); WHI findings do not support MHT for chronic disease prevention. Skin benefit is secondary and never on its own an indication (Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide).
Low-dose vaginal estrogen is effective for moderate-to-severe genitourinary syndrome of menopause without an added progestogen — the one setting where estrogen is given for the tissue itself.

Skin-directed care with stronger evidence: daily broad-spectrum sunscreen reduced measured skin ageing over 4.5 years in a 903-person independent RCT, and in the US one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for mitigating fine facial wrinkles (its label states it does not eliminate wrinkles or reverse photoaging).

In a consecutive NIH series of 32 people with MEN1, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas (identical to those of tuberous sclerosis) and 72% collagenomas; angiofibromas outside tuberous sclerosis warrant biochemical testing for MEN1.

Carney complex (over 70% carry inactivating PRKAR1A variants) presents with lentigines typically on the face, lips and mucosa (canthal pigmentation is seen only in Carney complex and Peutz–Jeghers syndrome), blue naevi and cutaneous myxomas (eyelid, ear, nipple); cardiac myxomas occur in 20–40% and cause more than half of disease mortality, which is why early detection and echocardiographic screening matter.
In MEN2A, cutaneous lichen amyloidosis — most often over the scapular upper back — clusters with RET codon-634 variants and is typically detected before medullary thyroid cancer.

Primary adrenal insufficiency causes hyperpigmentation particularly of sun-exposed areas, skin creases, mucosa and scars; the Endocrine Society recommends testing acutely ill patients with such signs and treating a suspected adrenal crisis before test results are available.

A rapid pace or progression of hirsutism, or virilization (clitoromegaly, deepening voice, increasing muscularity), points to a greater likelihood of an androgen-secreting neoplasm; the Endocrine Society suggests against androgen testing in women with regular cycles and unwanted local hair without an abnormal hirsutism score.

Other common endocrine skin signs: acanthosis nigricans tracks hyperinsulinaemia and insulin resistance; pretibial myxoedema reflects thyrotropin-receptor stimulation in Graves' disease; cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.

In the UK (product information checked 25 September 2026), HRT products such as estradiol patches (Evorel) and gel (Sandrena) are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms in peri- and postmenopausal women and, for some presentations, for preventing osteoporosis in postmenopausal women at high risk of fracture who cannot take other medicines approved for it; skin is not among their licensed uses.

In the UK, a hormone preparation compounded in a pharmacy or made as a 'special' is an unlicensed medicine; MHRA guidance says an unlicensed product should not be supplied where a licensed product can meet the patient's need, and a UK-licensed product used off-label comes before an unlicensed one.

On the UK electronic medicines compendium (searched 25 September 2026), topical tretinoin appears only in acne treatments: Treclin gel (clindamycin with tretinoin) and Aknemycin Plus (erythromycin with tretinoin); the other tretinoin product listed is an oral capsule.

Dermal white adipose tissue is a distinct adipocyte layer in the reticular dermis. In mice it expands after Staphylococcus aureus infection and its adipocytes release cathelicidin, and this antimicrobial capacity declines with age through TGF-β signalling. In human skin the layer is arranged in cones around pilosebaceous units, and human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that express cathelicidin; its contribution to human skin ageing has not been measured.
The subcutaneous fat of the face is partitioned into discrete anatomical compartments, and facial ageing is in part how these compartments change.
In 186 pairs of identical twins, a four-point higher BMI was associated with an older appearance before about age 40 and a younger appearance after 40.

Glycation proceeds non-enzymatically from Schiff base to Amadori product to advanced glycation end products (AGEs); AGEs cross-link long-lived collagen and, through RAGE, activate inflammatory signalling in laboratory and animal studies. A&RE rates the structural and inflammatory claims GRADE B; the course grades the causal link to visible skin ageing D because the human evidence is associative.

In human skin biopsies, collagen glycoxidation products (CML, pentosidine) and collagen fluorescence rise about five-fold between ages 20 and 85 and are up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes; human skin collagen has an estimated half-life of about 15 years.
Skin autofluorescence correlates moderately (r = 0.47–0.62) with skin-biopsy AGE measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin; it is a surrogate reading of AGE load.

Products sold as 'anti-glycation' are tested on surrogate readings or appearance scores; A&RE rates them GRADE C on surrogate endpoints, and no trial found for this course measured collagen cross-links in human skin.

GLP-1 and GIP are incretins that amplify glucose-dependent insulin secretion; GLP-1 also slows gastric emptying and reduces food intake, and native GLP-1 is degraded within minutes. Semaglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist; tirzepatide is a dual GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist.

US status as of September 2026: semaglutide is approved as Ozempic for type 2 diabetes (2017; label adds cardiovascular and kidney risk reduction in type 2 diabetes) and as Wegovy for chronic weight management (June 2021; adolescents from 12, December 2022), cardiovascular risk reduction in established CVD with obesity or overweight (March 2024) and noncirrhotic MASH with F2–F3 fibrosis (accelerated approval, August 2025); tirzepatide is approved as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes (2022; label adds cardiovascular risk reduction) and as Zepbound for chronic weight management (November 2023) and moderate-to-severe obstructive sleep apnoea with obesity (December 2024). No label includes a facial or skin-ageing indication.

In STEP-1 (1,961 adults without diabetes, 68 weeks) mean body-weight change was −14.9% with semaglutide vs −2.4% with placebo; in SURMOUNT-1 (2,539 adults, 72 weeks) it was −15.0% to −20.9% across tirzepatide doses vs −3.1% with placebo. Both guides grade weight management A.

Across 35 randomized trials of incretin drugs, a median of about 28% (IQR 16–40%) of the weight lost was muscle-related tissue, and no trial reported objective physical function; the US labels state that fat mass loss exceeds lean mass loss.

Human evidence on facial change during incretin-driven weight loss is observational and small: a retrospective imaging study of 20 patients found a median 9% loss of midface volume, mostly superficial and about 7% per 10 kg lost, and a survey of 1,226 patients found self-reported sagging, facial volume loss and hair loss rising with the percentage of weight lost. A systematic review found the plastic-surgery literature limited by bias. No randomized trial has measured facial fat, laxity or appearance as an outcome of semaglutide or tirzepatide (PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov, September 2026); registered randomized trials test fillers and devices in people already on these drugs.

The US labels list hair loss among common adverse reactions — Wegovy 3.3% vs 1% placebo (higher at the higher approved dose), Zepbound about 4–5% vs 1% — more frequent in women and associated with weight reduction; the Wegovy label also lists dysesthesia (altered skin sensation). Neither label lists facial volume loss. Telogen effluvium after rapid weight loss is the proposed mechanism.
Whether GLP-1 receptor agonists act directly on facial fat or dermal cells, independent of weight loss, rests on cell and animal studies and has not been tested in people.

In the US, compounded, counterfeit and falsely labelled 'research' semaglutide and tirzepatide are not FDA-approved, and FDA has warned about each (page current 1 September 2026); semaglutide bought online without a prescription has failed independent testing.

Management of facial change during incretin therapy is counselling before treatment (the Hormonaly guide advises raising facial volume and laxity, especially with older patients), monitoring with consented photographs, support for protein intake and resistance training to protect lean mass (guide advice), and referral to a qualified aesthetic clinician for restoration. Published restoration advice is expert opinion (the main consensus statement was developed with industry involvement), and randomized filler and device trials in these patients have no results yet. Decisions about the medicine belong to the prescriber and patient.

Inflammaging is chronic, low-grade, sterile inflammation that rises with age; raised inflammatory markers such as IL-6 and CRP predict morbidity, disability, frailty and death in older adults. Increased gut permeability is one proposed source.

Metabolic endotoxaemia is shown in mice (high-fat feeding raises plasma LPS; LPS infusion reproduces weight gain and insulin resistance) and as a transient rise in plasma endotoxin after a high-fat meal in 12 healthy men. Measuring intestinal permeability is complex, a leading review concludes it is unproven that restoring barrier function improves gastrointestinal or systemic disease, and a widely used commercial zonulin ELISA does not detect zonulin. Whether a leaky gut drives skin disease in people has not been shown.

In a Cochrane review of 39 RCTs (2,599 participants), probiotics probably make little or no difference to patient-rated eczema symptoms, and the combined severity score fell by less than the minimum clinically important difference; a 2024 EAACI meta-analysis of 20 RCTs in children without food allergy reported a significant SCORAD reduction. Probiotic effects are strain-specific.

Other gut- and metabolism-directed skin evidence: rosacea improved after rifaximin eradication of small-intestinal bacterial overgrowth in a small single-centre RCT (C); an 8-week placebo-controlled RCT of liraglutide in 20 people with psoriasis found no effect (C); an open-label, manufacturer-sponsored phase 3b RCT (274 people) found more complete psoriasis clearance when tirzepatide was added to ixekizumab (C), and tirzepatide has no psoriasis indication in the US. A fibre-rich diet has strong human evidence for cardiometabolic outcomes (A&RE A; the review's own certainty moderate) and no skin-outcome trials; an Akkermansia pilot RCT in 32 adults improved insulin sensitivity (C). A&RE grades the 'leaky gut' repair stack (L-glutamine, zinc carnosine, BPC-157) D, and as of September 2026 BPC-157 is not on the US 503A bulks list after the July 2026 PCAC review.

In the UK (product information checked 25 September 2026), Ozempic (semaglutide) is licensed for type 2 diabetes; Wegovy (semaglutide) for weight management in adults and adolescents and for reducing major adverse cardiovascular events in adults with established cardiovascular disease and obesity or overweight; and Mounjaro (tirzepatide), under one brand, for type 2 diabetes and for weight management, the weight indication having been authorised by MHRA on 8 November 2023. Psoriasis is not a UK indication for tirzepatide.
UK product information lists hair loss for Wegovy (2.5% on semaglutide vs 1.0% on placebo) and Mounjaro (4.9% on tirzepatide vs 1.0% on placebo in the pooled weight-management studies).

MHRA stated on 24 July 2026 that retatrutide has not been authorised for use in the UK and that anyone selling it does so illegally; on 28 May 2026 it made its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines (around 12,000 doses, including retatrutide, tirzepatide and peptide products).

In the UK, an unlicensed medicine may be supplied as a 'special' only to meet an individual patient's special clinical need that no licensed product can meet (not for cost or convenience), on the order of a prescriber who takes responsibility for prescribing it and for the patient's follow-up.
GHK is an endogenous human plasma tripeptide first described in 1973; GHK-Cu is its copper complex.

Proposed mechanism: GHK-Cu modulates copper delivery to enzymes including superoxide dismutase and lysyl oxidase and activates wound-healing and antioxidant gene-expression programmes — a mechanistic claim resting on reviews by the peptide's originator.

Human evidence for topical GHK-Cu is small-trial: one PubMed-indexed randomized trial (post-laser wound healing, 2006) and manufacturer-sponsored cosmetic trials that are not indexed; the guides rate the cosmetic indication GRADE C.
Injectable GHK-Cu has no randomized human trials; use rests on anecdote, and injection-site pain and rash are common.
Whether topical GHK-Cu reaches the dermis in meaningful amounts is unsettled; penetration data are in vitro and measurement-dependent.

US status (as of May 14, 2026): GHK-Cu for non-injectable routes sits in FDA's 503A Category 1 (under evaluation) after its nomination was withdrawn on April 22, 2026 and partially reinstated; FDA intends to consult the PCAC on it before the end of February 2027. Category 1 is an enforcement posture, not approval; the injectable route has no such standing.

Palmitoyl pentapeptide-4 (pal-KTTKS, Matrixyl) improved photoaging measures in a 12-week randomized trial funded by the manufacturer; the Matrixyl 3000 blend rests on the maker's technical dossier, which is not indexed.

Argireline (acetyl hexapeptide-3/-8) mimics the N-terminus of SNAP-25; randomized placebo-controlled trials report modest wrinkle improvement, but delivery to the neuromuscular junction at cosmetic concentrations is considered implausible — the effect, if real, is not a botulinum substitute.

Leuphasyl (pentapeptide-18): the efficacy data are the manufacturer's own studies, an in-vitro synergy figure with SNAP-8, and one small uncontrolled university volunteer study (2014, in a journal not indexed in PubMed). No randomized controlled trial exists. The course grades it D.
Cosmetic peptides are regulated as cosmetic ingredients, not drugs, and their safety is evaluated by a cosmetics framework rather than a drug-approval pathway.

BPC-157 evidence is an extensive rodent literature, largely from one research group, plus uncontrolled human case series. No randomized efficacy trial in people has been published in full: the one randomized trial FDA identified (ulcerative colitis, 2005) exists only as a meeting abstract and showed no significant difference from placebo; a 2015 phase 1 safety study and a 2025 single-arm product study posted no results; a randomized phase 1 trial after rotator-cuff repair was registered in 2026, starting 2027.

TB-500 is the acetylated 17–23 fragment of thymosin β4 (Ac-LKKTETQ), not thymosin β4 itself; the fragment was characterized by analysing the product, and human trial data for the fragment do not exist.
KPV, the C-terminal tripeptide of α-MSH, reduces inflammation in murine colitis models; no randomized human trials exist for any indication.

Topical LL-37 has two randomized placebo-controlled trials in hard-to-heal venous leg ulcers: a small first-in-human dose-ranging trial (n=34) that was positive at low dose, and a larger phase IIb trial that was negative in its full cohort — a worked example of why a small positive trial is not confirmation.

BPC-157, KPV and TB-500 (with MOTS-c, emideltide, semax and epitalon) were reviewed by FDA's Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee on July 23–24, 2026 for possible addition to the 503A bulks list; the committee's votes are advisory, FDA rulemaking is still required, and compounding these substances without bulks-list standing has drawn FDA warning letters.

Research-use-only peptide products are made outside GMP. Impurity, inaccurate content and contamination are documented for adjacent products — seized 'research' peptides and online semaglutide — but no published analysis of skin-peptide RUO products was found. Heavy-metal contamination is reported for this market, not documented; the lesson says exactly that.
GLOW (GHK-Cu + BPC-157 + TB-500) and KLOW (+ KPV) are marketing names for research-use-only blends with no controlled human trials.

Oral collagen peptides: pooled randomized trials report better hydration, elasticity and wrinkle scores, and A&RE rates the evidence GRADE C — but in a 2025 meta-analysis of 23 RCTs (1,474 participants) stratified by funding and quality, the benefit appeared only in pharmaceutical-funded and low-quality trials; unfunded and high-quality trials showed no effect.
In the US oral collagen is sold as a dietary supplement: it may not carry disease claims, and product quality and content vary.

SNAP-8 (acetyl octapeptide-1/-3) is the manufacturer's eight-residue extension of the Argireline SNAP-25 mimic. Its efficacy figures come from the manufacturer; the only indexed human studies test it inside multi-ingredient microneedle patches, so no study isolates its effect.

In Great Britain, a product applied to the external parts of the body mainly to clean, perfume, change the appearance of, protect or keep them in good condition is a cosmetic under the assimilated Cosmetic Products Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, which excludes anything intended to be ingested, inhaled, injected or implanted; before it is made available, its UK Responsible Person must hold a safety assessment by a qualified assessor and notify OPSS, and must be able to prove the claims made for it, which may not imply characteristics the product does not have.

In the UK, oral collagen sold in dose form is regulated as a food supplement; food information may not attribute to any food the property of preventing, treating or curing a human disease, and a health claim may be used only if it is authorised and on the Great Britain register.

On 13 May 2026 the UK Advertising Standards Authority upheld a complaint that the claim 'Clinically proven To Lift The Skin By 20%' for a serum containing a lifting peptide complex was misleading: the study behind it had 30 participants, no placebo or control group and a subjective grading score.

In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicine from its claims (including websites and social media), presentation, product form and use; a medicinal product with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or offered for sale (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, reg. 46) or advertised (reg. 279) unless an exemption applies. MHRA's largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines (28 May 2026) included peptide products.

Human scalp hair follicles kept alive ex vivo respond to CRH by making POMC products (ACTH, α-MSH) and secreting cortisol, with HPA-like negative feedback, and ex vivo they also operate a GH/IGF-1-like somatotropic loop — a mechanism from organ-culture studies.
Androgenetic alopecia is mediated by dihydrotestosterone: locally, 5α-reductase converts testosterone to DHT, which miniaturises genetically susceptible scalp follicles.
Growing (anagen) hair follicles are immune-privileged; collapse of that privilege, with NKG2D+ CD8 T-cell and NK-cell infiltration of the bulb, is an essential prerequisite for alopecia areata.

In two phase 3 RCTs (BRAVE-AA1 and -AA2; 1,200 adults with severe alopecia areata; funded by Eli Lilly), baricitinib was superior to placebo: 38.8% and 35.9% on the higher dose reached SALT ≤20 at week 36, versus 6.2% and 3.3% on placebo. In the US, FDA approved baricitinib for adults with severe alopecia areata on 13 June 2022.

The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide's first-pass hair-loss workup: patterned thinning → androgenetic alopecia (topical minoxidil; finasteride in men; treat coexisting iron or thyroid problems); diffuse shedding after a trigger → telogen effluvium (remove the trigger, reassure, recheck ferritin and TSH); patchy smooth loss (± nail pitting) → alopecia areata (dermatology referral; screen thyroid and autoimmune disease); signs of androgen excess → hyperandrogenism work-up; always ferritin and TSH, androgens if virilising, biopsy a scarring pattern; refer severe or rapidly progressive alopecia areata promptly.
A systematic review and meta-analysis of good- or fair-quality RCTs found topical minoxidil (in men and in women) and oral finasteride (in men) superior to placebo for androgenetic alopecia.

In the US (Drugs@FDA, checked 24 September 2026), topical minoxidil has been approved since 1988 and is marketed over the counter; finasteride for hair loss (Propecia) has been a prescription drug since 1997.

Skin cells produce POMC and its products ACTH, α-MSH and β-endorphin and carry their receptors. Of the five melanocortin receptors, MC1R mediates pigmentation of skin and hair, MC2R adrenal steroidogenesis, MC3R and MC4R central control of food intake, and MC5R sebogenesis; true receptor distribution is probably wider than this map.

Afamelanotide is an MC1R agonist. In two sponsor-funded phase 3 RCTs in erythropoietic protoporphyria it increased pain-free time in direct sunlight (US trial, n=94: median 69.4 vs 40.8 hours over six months; EU trial, n=74: 6.0 vs 0.8 hours over nine months, with fewer phototoxic reactions). Both guides grade it A for EPP. Use outside EPP remains investigational (for example a phase 3 vitiligo trial started in 2023 with no results posted).

Afamelanotide (Scenesse) was authorised in the EU on 22 December 2014, under exceptional circumstances, for prevention of phototoxicity in adults with EPP, and approved in the US in 2019 to increase pain-free light exposure in adults with a history of phototoxic reactions from EPP. The current US label (revised August 2024) warns it may darken pre-existing naevi and freckles and recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.

Melanotan II is a non-selective melanocortin agonist (MC1R, MC3R, MC4R, MC5R) that crosses into the brain. Its only controlled human data are a 1996 single-blind pilot in three men (tanning in two; nausea, yawning, spontaneous erections, somnolence) and a 1998 crossover in ten men with psychogenic erectile dysfunction; no trial has tested cosmetic tanning. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it C and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide D ('harms > benefit'); the course grades cosmetic use D.

Reported harms of Melanotan II come from case reports and reviews: darkening and growth of existing naevi, eruptive and atypical (dysplastic) naevi, melanonychia; at least five melanomas reported during or after use, each in a person with other risk factors, so causation is unproven; ischaemic priapism needing surgery; sympathomimetic toxicity with rhabdomyolysis and renal dysfunction; FDA also lists posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome among published serious events.

Melanotan II sold online is of uncertain content: vials from three online shops held 43–88% of the labelled amount, with up to 5.9% unknown impurities, and TGA testing of five identically labelled seized nasal sprays found content varying more than twofold between bottles.

Melanotan II is approved for no therapeutic indication. US: FDA's compounding safety page (current as of 22 April 2026) lists it among nominations withdrawn from Category 2, citing impurity and immunogenicity risks and published reports of melanoma, PRES, sympathomimetic toxidrome and priapism. UK: MHRA (FOI 24/274, 17 April 2024) classes injectable products as medicines, says unauthorised medicines may not be sold, supplied or advertised, and advises users to stop immediately. Australia: TGA (17 August 2026) — prescription-only medicine, not approved as a tanning agent, no product on the ARTG.

The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats a personal or family history of melanoma as an absolute contraindication to Melanotan II. A case report describes crops of new atypical naevi and growth of existing naevi in a man with prior melanoma who self-injected an α-MSH analogue, with lightening after he stopped; MC1R activation does not prevent melanoma, and regular skin examination remains critical in high-risk people.

Skin monitoring matters with melanocortin agonists: during Melanotan II use, sequential videodermoscopy documented naevus changes that made naevus and melanoma hard to tell apart, and even the approved MC1R agonist's US label recommends a full-body skin examination twice yearly.

PTD-DBM is a cell-penetrating peptide that competes CXXC5 off Dishevelled, activating Wnt/β-catenin; in mice it accelerated hair regrowth and wound-induced follicle neogenesis, and CXXC5 is raised in human balding scalp. This single 2017 study from the developer's group is its whole evidence: no human trial is published (PubMed) or registered (ClinicalTrials.gov) as of 24 September 2026. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

A 2025 review's abstract speaks of 'clinical efficacy' for peptides such as PTD-DBM, but its own table describes PTD-DBM as unapproved and shown in mouse models, and flags an untested theoretical risk: off-target Wnt activation is associated with colorectal and hepatocellular carcinomas.

Thymulin is a thymic peptide that is biologically active only when zinc-bound. No indexed human study of zinc thymulin for hair was found (the Peptide Pocket Guide's cited case series could not be located); its proposed hair mechanism is undefined, and whether any effect comes from the peptide or the zinc is unresolved. The Peptide Pocket Guide grades it D.

In the US, on FDA's 503A category lists of 14 May 2026, thymulin acetate sits in Category 3 (nominated without adequate support, not eligible for the Category 1 policy) and PTD-DBM appears in no category; neither is on the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23).

In the UK, baricitinib (Olumiant) is a prescription-only medicine licensed for severe alopecia areata in adults; NICE (TA926, 25 October 2023) did not recommend it for NHS use because the cost-effectiveness estimates were uncertain and higher than NICE normally accepts.

In the UK, topical minoxidil is licensed for androgenetic alopecia and Regaine for Men Extra Strength Scalp Foam 5% is on the General Sales List; finasteride for hair loss (Propecia) is a prescription-only medicine licensed for male pattern hair loss in men, is not prescribed on the NHS and is available only by private prescription.

On 11 May 2026 MHRA strengthened its warnings that finasteride is associated with depression, suicidal ideation and sexual dysfunction that may persist after treatment stops; it advises prescribers to inform patients when prescribing, point them to the patient card, ask about a history of depression or suicidal ideation, and review them regularly for psychiatric and sexual side effects.

In the UK, afamelanotide has a marketing authorisation under exceptional circumstances for preventing phototoxicity in adults with erythropoietic protoporphyria, to be prescribed only by specialist clinicians in recognised porphyria centres; NICE (HST27, 26 July 2023) did not recommend it for NHS use.

In the UK, a medicine made up for one patient without a marketing authorisation is an unlicensed 'special'; MHRA guidance says an unlicensed product should not be used where a UK-licensed product could meet the patient's need, and special need excludes cost, convenience and operational reasons.

Growth hormone acts mainly in the dermis: its receptor is expressed more by dermal fibroblasts than keratinocytes, and GH increases fibroblast numbers and supports collagen synthesis. IGF-1, made locally by fibroblasts and melanocytes, acts on keratinocytes through the IGF-1 receptor; in culture IGF-1, not GH, drives keratinocyte proliferation.
Human hair follicles operate a functional peripheral equivalent of the somatotropic (GHRH–GH–IGF-1) axis ex vivo.
GH secretion and IGF-1 decline progressively with age (the somatopause); IGF-1 must be read against age- and sex-adjusted ranges, so a value low for a young adult is often normal for age.

Human skin reflects the axis at its extremes: adults with GH deficiency have a thinner epidermis and reduced sweating on biopsy, not fully reversed by treatment of childhood-onset deficiency; in acromegaly, dermal glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema thicken and puff the skin of the face, hands and feet.

In people with burns over 40% of body surface, recombinant GH shortened burn-wound and donor-site healing in pooled small randomized trials (13 RCTs, 701 people), with more hyperglycaemia; the evidence carries risk of bias.

A much-cited 1990 NEJM study gave GH to 12 healthy men over 60 with nine untreated men as comparison and no placebo; skin thickness rose 7.1% (P = 0.07, not significant). A 1996 RCT in 28 older men found 15% more collagen deposited in implanted wound tubes on GH — a laboratory surrogate.

In healthy older adults, randomized trials of GH show small body-composition changes (about 2 kg less fat, 2 kg more lean mass) with more oedema, arthralgia, carpal tunnel syndrome and gynaecomastia and a trend to diabetes, while strength and endurance change little; GH is not recommended as anti-ageing therapy. A&RE grades this advice A; on the course rule the trials give B, with the same conclusion.

In the US (21 U.S.C. 333(e), current text read September 2026), knowingly distributing human growth hormone for any use other than treating a disease or recognized condition authorised by FDA, on a physician's order, is a federal offence.

Tesamorelin, a GHRH analogue, reduced visceral fat by about 15% versus placebo at 26 weeks in two developer-run phase 3 RCTs (806 patients pooled), with subcutaneous fat unchanged; in the US it has been FDA-approved since 2010 for reduction of excess abdominal fat in HIV-infected adults with lipodystrophy, and its label excludes weight loss. Both guides grade it A — for that indication only.

Tesamorelin's label reports IGF-1 above +2 SDS in 47% (above +3 SDS in 36%) of treated patients at 26 weeks, states that the effects of prolonged IGF-1 elevation are unknown, reports diabetes-range HbA1c in 5% vs 1% on placebo, lists fluid retention, and contraindicates use in active malignancy.

A PubMed search in September 2026 found no randomized trial with a skin outcome for tesamorelin, CJC-1295, ipamorelin or IGF-1 LR3; the closest human skin data for a GHRH analogue are a 1997 single-blind study of [Nle27]GHRH(1-29) in 19 older adults, with caliper skin thickness rising after a placebo lead-in and no parallel control.

CJC-1295 with DAC raised GH and IGF-1 for days in phase 1 trials in healthy adults, with no clinical endpoint; CJC-1295 without DAC ('Mod GRF 1-29') and IGF-1 LR3 have no peer-reviewed human studies. The Hormonaly guides rate CJC-1295/ipamorelin C ('anecdotal'); on the course rule the evidence for any clinical or skin benefit is D.

Ipamorelin's only efficacy RCT (postoperative ileus, phase 2) showed no benefit over placebo; ibutamoren (MK-677) raised GH, IGF-1 and fat-free mass in a 2-year RCT in older adults without improving strength or function, raised fasting glucose and lowered insulin sensitivity, and a hip-fracture phase IIb trial was stopped early for a heart-failure signal.

In the US, sermorelin was approved as Geref (1990, diagnostic; 1997, idiopathic GH deficiency in children), discontinued in 2008, and its approvals withdrawn in 2009 at the maker's request; FDA determined in 2013 that this was not for safety or effectiveness reasons. As of 24 September 2026 no sermorelin product is marketed (Drugs@FDA), and sermorelin appears in no 503A category (FDA list of 14 May 2026).

US compounding status (FDA 503A category list of 14 May 2026; Category 2 page current 22 April 2026; 21 CFR 216.23 as of September 2026): no GH-axis peptide is on the 503A bulks list; ibutamoren is in 503A and 503B Category 2; GHRP-2 and GHRP-6 are in 503A Category 3 and 503B Category 2; CJC-1295 and ipamorelin are listed among withdrawn Category 2 nominations, with ipamorelin still in 503B Category 2; FDA's advisory committee voted against ibutamoren (1–13) and ipamorelin (0–12, 1 abstention) in October 2024; a 2020 warning letter named CJC 1295, ipamorelin, IGF1-LR3, GHRP-2, GHRP-6 and MK 677 as ineligible for 503A exemptions.

Skin and soft-tissue signs of GH excess include puffiness and thickening of the face, hands and feet from glycosaminoglycan deposition and oedema, oily skin with large pores, hyperhidrosis, skin tags and acanthosis nigricans, with slow acral and jaw enlargement; the Endocrine Society recommends IGF-1 measurement for typical acral and facial features and suggests it when several associated conditions cluster (sleep apnoea, type 2 diabetes, debilitating arthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome, hyperhidrosis, hypertension).

GH-axis drugs commonly cause fluid retention (oedema, arthralgia, paraesthesia, carpal tunnel symptoms), usually transient and dose-related, and glucose intolerance; somatropin labelling asks that pre-existing nevi be monitored for growth or malignant change.

Observed human data on IGF-1 and cancer are associations: higher circulating IGF-1 is linked with modestly higher risks of prostate, breast, colorectal and thyroid cancer, with reverse causation not excluded; acromegaly shows a slightly raised cancer incidence in pooled studies (SIR 1.5) that a nationwide cohort did not confirm (SIR 1.1).

GH treatment cohorts are largely reassuring for replacement: no clear raised cancer risk in 23,984 GH-treated children with growth failure and no other major disease, and a 2022 consensus found no association between GH replacement and primary tumour or recurrence; people with GH-receptor deficiency have very little cancer. No long-term cancer data exist for secretagogues or IGF-1 LR3 used for ageing or skin — the mitogenic risk there is plausible and unmeasured.

In the UK, somatropin (for example Genotropin) is a prescription-only medicine licensed in children for growth disturbance from growth hormone deficiency, Turner syndrome, chronic renal insufficiency, short stature after small-for-gestational-age birth and Prader-Willi syndrome, and in adults for pronounced growth hormone deficiency; somatropin is a Class C controlled drug under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971.

A search of MHRA's products database on 25 September 2026 returned no summary of product characteristics, patient leaflet or public assessment report for tesamorelin, sermorelin or ipamorelin; supplied in the UK, any of them would be an unlicensed medicine, which MHRA guidance reserves for an individual patient's special need that no licensed product meets.

GRADE rates certainty in four levels (high, moderate, low, very low) for an outcome across a body of evidence, not for a single study or a molecule; randomized trials start high and observational studies start low.

Certainty is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (unexplained variability across studies), indirectness (study PICO differs from the question), imprecision (confidence interval crossing the important-difference threshold) and suspected publication bias — which a body of small, industry-funded studies should raise — and can be rated up for large effects.

Applied to this course: topical GHK-Cu's only indexed RCT measured post-laser healing (indirect for photoageing); BPC-157 wound data are rodent models (indirect); LL-37's 34-person positive trial and 148-person negative phase IIb disagree (inconsistent); oral collagen's benefit disappears in high-quality trials (risk of bias).

A Cochrane methodology review of 75 papers found industry-sponsored drug and device studies more often reported favourable efficacy results (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.17–1.37; moderate-quality evidence) and favourable conclusions (RR 1.34) than non-industry studies, a bias not explained by standard risk-of-bias assessment.

Both Hormonaly guides attach an A–D letter to the evidence for a specific use — adapted from GRADE's four levels — which rates evidence, not legality; mechanistic appeal never raises a grade, and grade and regulatory status are separate checks to clear.

In the US, 503A compounding by a licensed pharmacist or physician for an identified patient is exempt from new-drug approval, adequate directions for use and cGMP only if the bulk substance meets a USP/NF monograph, or failing that is a component of an approved drug, or failing that is on the 503A bulks list — and is made by an FDA-registered establishment and accompanied by a valid certificate of analysis. Quality is defined by reference to those standards and the certificate, not by a numerical purity threshold in the statute's text.

503B outsourcing facilities compound sterile drugs, register with FDA, must meet cGMP, are inspected on a risk-based schedule, report adverse events and may compound without patient-specific prescriptions; their products are exempt from approval and adequate-directions requirements, so they remain unapproved.
As of 22 September 2026 the 503A bulks list (21 CFR 216.23) holds six substances, none a peptide, unchanged since 2019; listing carries no FDA endorsement of safety or efficacy.

Categories 1–3 are FDA's interim enforcement posture while nominations are evaluated, not listing. As of 14 May 2026 Category 1 includes GHK-Cu except injectable routes and 503A Category 2 holds six substances; BPC-157, TB-500, KPV, injectable GHK-Cu, LL-37 and melanotan II sit in a table of withdrawn nominations whose safety concerns remain posted.

The July 2026 Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee is advisory; FDA's review staff concluded the listing criteria weigh against BPC-157, and only rulemaking changes the bulks list, which no rule had changed as of September 2026.

Since 23 March 2020 FDA defines a protein as an alpha amino acid polymer of more than 40 amino acids, chemically synthesized or not, so such products are biological products; tesamorelin and hyaluronidase were deemed biologics licences on that date, and biologics are not eligible for the 503A or 503B compounding exemptions.

How residues are counted can decide classification: a federal district court in 2025 upheld FDA's determination that retatrutide (39-alpha-amino-acid backbone plus a two-residue side chain) is not a protein, remanding only the 'analogous to a protein' question; the appeal was pending as of the latest filings found (June 2026).

A certificate of analysis is the supplier's attestation for a named lot — mass spectrometry for identity (observed against expected mass), HPLC for purity, plus endotoxin, microbial, water, counter-ion, metal and solvent results. It cannot establish that the vial in hand is that lot, how it was stored since testing, or that the product is sterile and suitable to inject; lot-less, chromatogram-less, stale (over 12 months) and endotoxin-less certificates are warning signs.

There is no single universal endotoxin limit per milligram: FDA's guidance says the limit is calculated with the USP method from the product's dosage regimen and strength, and some routes (intrathecal, ophthalmic) differ.

FDA's July 2026 briefing on BPC-157 found the nominators' certificates described a different form (the acetate) from the one nominated, that publicly available BPC-157 certificates mostly report purity alone with no impurity limits, and that the nominator's certificate mentioned no endotoxin test.

Paperwork and contents can diverge: three semaglutide vials bought from illegal online pharmacies measured 7.7–14.4% purity against 99% on the label, 29–39% more peptide than labelled and endotoxin in every vial; a seized injection vial held an undocumented GHRP-2 analogue identifiable only by high-resolution mass spectrometry. Neither study concerns skin peptides.

'Not for use in humans' research labelling (21 CFR 312.160) permits shipment only for laboratory or in-vitro research, and FDA reads intended use objectively from claims, advertising and the circumstances of distribution (21 CFR 201.128); a research-use-only product therefore has no clinical route, and a certificate does not create one.

In the US the regime follows intended use and route: appearance claims make a cosmetic (no premarket approval), while a claim to affect structure or function — such as 'regenerate cells' — makes a drug, and 'cosmeceutical' has no legal meaning; dietary supplements are not approved before sale, their makers being responsible for safety and labelling.

'Off-label' describes unapproved use of an approved drug; a never-approved peptide has no label to depart from, introducing an unapproved new drug into interstate commerce is a prohibited act under the FD&C Act, and FDA has warned a compounding pharmacy that its BPC-157 and GHK-Cu products did not qualify for the 503A exemptions.

For an unapproved or compounded peptide the chart should name the article and its regulatory status in those terms; if compounded, the pathway, facility and certificate relied on; consent covering non-approval, foreseeable risks, approved alternatives (including doing nothing) and what happens if harm occurs — elements the Peptide Pocket Guide borrows from FDA's research-consent rule; the evidence grade quoted; monitoring and a stopping rule; and the date the FDA lists were checked.

In the UK, regulation 167 of the Human Medicines Regulations 2012 lifts the marketing-authorisation requirement (regulation 46) for a 'special' supplied in response to an unsolicited order, manufactured to the specification of a doctor, dentist, nurse independent prescriber, pharmacist independent prescriber or supplementary prescriber, for a patient under that person's direct responsibility, to meet the patient's special needs; no advertisement may be published, and UK manufacture requires a manufacturer's licence for special medicinal products.

MHRA Guidance Note 14: specials are made in GMP-inspected facilities but are otherwise unassessed for safety, quality and efficacy; an unlicensed product should not be supplied where a licensed product can meet the patient's special need, and special need excludes cost, convenience and operational reasons; the order of preference is a UK-licensed product (even off-label), then a product licensed in its country of origin, then a UK special, with products that are not medicines in their country of origin, such as supplements, least acceptable.

A pharmacist may also prepare or dispense a medicinal product in a registered pharmacy, hospital or health centre in accordance with a prescription without a marketing authorisation (Medicines Act 1968, s. 10); MHRA counts such pharmacy preparations among unlicensed medicines.

UK professional guidance puts responsibility for an unlicensed medicine on its prescriber: GMC — be satisfied there is sufficient evidence or experience of safety and efficacy, take responsibility for prescribing and for overseeing care and follow-up, record the reasons when not following common practice, and explain to the patient when the use is not routine or licensed alternatives exist; MHRA advises the same and names doctors, dentists, independent nurse and pharmacist prescribers and, in some circumstances, supplementary prescribers as able to prescribe unlicensed medicines; the GPhC asks pharmacist prescribers to be sure of sufficient evidence and to record discussions and reasons; the NMC Code limits prescribing to the registrant's training, competence, the law and guidance.

In the UK, MHRA decides whether a product is a medicinal product from all its claims (including websites and social media), its presentation, its product form (such as injection) and the way it is used; a medicinal product with no UK marketing authorisation may not be sold, supplied or offered for sale (Human Medicines Regulations 2012, reg. 46) or advertised (reg. 279).

MHRA classifies injectable melanotan products as medicines and has removed melanotan products from the market (FOI 24/274, April 2024); its largest seizure of unlicensed weight-loss medicines, on 28 May 2026, included peptide products.

UK law prohibits publishing an advertisement likely to lead to the use of a prescription-only medicine (reg. 284), and CAP Code rule 12.12 bars advertising prescription-only medicines to the public; MHRA's Blue Guide lets clinics promote a service such as 'treatment for lines and wrinkles' provided they do not name a prescription-only medicine, and says unlicensed medicines should not be mentioned.

On 11 February 2026 the ASA upheld a complaint that Instagram posts by customers of an online pharmacy's referral scheme, carrying discount codes and hashtags such as '#mounjaro', promoted a prescription-only medicine to the public.

GMC guidance for doctors who offer cosmetic interventions requires a physical examination before prescribing injectable cosmetic medicines, which therefore may not be prescribed by telephone, video link or online for patients the doctor has not examined.

Lesson 1.1 The skin as a steroidogenic, endocrine organ · Lesson 1.2 Receptor maps and what they prove · Lesson 1.3 Senescence, the SASP and the ageing dermis.
Module 01 · The skin as an endocrine organ
The skin makes its own hormones.
This course starts with physiology, because every later question about a hormone or peptide for skin rests on it. Skin senses hormones from the blood, makes several of its own, and ages in ways that change both. In three lessons you will separate what happens locally in the skin from what the rest of the body sends in, and label each finding by the kind of evidence behind it.

Lesson 1.1 · Concept
Four units, one circuit.
Recent reviews describe the skin as a neuro-immuno-endocrine organ built from four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal (hair follicles and glands). Each holds cells that can make hormones and mount an immune response. They signal to neighbouring cells, through sensory nerves, and through the blood. Most of this picture comes from cell, tissue and animal studies.
Four units: epidermal, dermal, hypodermal, adnexal
Three routes: neighbour to neighbour, nerve, bloodstream
Mechanism register: cell, tissue and animal work
Narration: Think of the skin as a sensing organ with its own hormone supply. Researchers who study it describe four units, epidermal, dermal, hypodermal and adnexal, the last meaning hair follicles and glands. What changes in practice
Read the skin before the serum.
The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide treats the aesthetic exam as a systemic screen. Sudden thinning and easy bruising suggest cortisol excess; coarse, dry, cool skin suggests hypothyroidism; new acanthosis nigricans flags insulin resistance. It lists violaceous striae with new hypertension or diabetes, and rapidly progressive virilisation, among reasons to refer promptly to endocrinology. Local skin biology explains how skin behaves; it does not justify prescribing a hormone.
A skin sign can be the first sign of a systemic disorder
Some patterns need prompt endocrine referral
Local loops explain biology; they do not justify treatment

Lesson 1.2 · Concept
A map of fourteen million cells.
The Hormone Cell Atlas, published in Science in 2026, read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in about 14 million single cells and nuclei from 47 human tissues, skin among them. From that RNA it predicted which cell types could make a hormone and which could respond to one. It is a map of predicted capacity; it did not measure hormone release.
About 14 million cells and nuclei, 47 tissues
Output: predicted producers and receivers
Narration: Fourteen million cells is the scale of the Hormone Cell Atlas, a Cambridge-led study published in Science in 2026. The team read the RNA for 379 hormone and receptor genes in single cells and nuclei from forty-seven human tissues, skin included. From those readings they scored each cell type for its predicted capacity to make or to receive a hormone, and they flagged unexpected sites, such …

units.text:
What the atlas is
Prediction, in the authors' own words.
The atlas's own portal describes its scores as 'putative and hypothesis-generating'. A few predictions were tested in cells in the paper itself; the rest are left for users to validate. Across biology, the amount of RNA for a gene is often a poor guide to how much protein a cell makes, and protein is still a step short of secretion.
379
hormone and receptor genes read as RNA, cell by cell
Fei, Huang-Doran et al., Science 2026 · about 14 million cells and nuclei · 47 human tissues
What it means: The atlas shows which skin cells carry the RNA to make or sense a hormone. That is a well-founded hypothesis about where to look.
What it does not mean: It does not show that a skin cell secretes a hormone, how much, or that the hormone acts there. A receptor gene on the map is not evidence that a product aimed at it works.

What changes in practice
A map to confirm, then a trial.
Topical and transdermal treatments act through receptors the skin already carries, and the skin's own enzymes change how strongly a hormone acts, so the skin's response need not mirror the dose. A receptor on a map is where an efficacy question starts. The same caution applies to physiology you think you know: the guide says serum vitamin D falls with sunscreen use, yet field trials of daily sunscreen did not lower it.
A receptor on the map is a hypothesis
Local enzymes change potency in skin
Daily-sunscreen field trials did not lower vitamin D

A brochure for a hormone-containing serum cites a single-cell atlas showing that dermal fibroblasts carry the RNA for that hormone's receptor. What does that finding establish?
Explanation: A receptor on the map is where the question starts.
Distractor (deliberately false, not a claim): That the serum reaches those fibroblasts and improves the skin.
Explanation: That needs penetration data and a clinical trial; an RNA map provides neither.

Explanation: The finding concerns a receptor, and RNA says nothing about secretion or deficiency.
Correct answer: That fibroblasts may respond to the hormone: a hypothesis to confirm at the protein, function and clinical level.
Explanation: Correct. The atlas's authors call such predictions putative and hypothesis-generating.

Lesson 1.3 · Concept
Cells that stop dividing and keep talking.
A senescent cell has stopped dividing for good but stays metabolically active, releasing cytokines, matrix-degrading enzymes and growth factors: the senescence-associated secretory phenotype, or SASP. The SASP was characterised in cultured cells. In human skin, cells carrying the senescence marker p16INK4a become more common with age in both epidermis and dermis.
Senescent: permanent arrest, still secreting
SASP (IL-6, IL-8, MMPs, growth factors): defined in culture
Human skin: p16-positive cells rise with age
Narration: Senescence begins as a safety mechanism. A cell that has taken enough damage stops dividing for good, which helps guard against cancer and is useful during wound repair. The problem is what the cell does next. It stays alive and metabolically busy and releases a mixture of inflammatory cytokines such as inte…

Human evidence
Three years of perceived age.
In a Dutch cohort, people with more p16-positive cells in sun-protected arm skin had more ageing-type elastic fibres, more facial wrinkles and looked older, after allowing for their actual age. The epidermal p16-positive cells were mostly melanocytes. The study was publicly funded; one co-author worked for Unilever.
3 years
younger-looking: fewest versus most p16-positive epidermal cells, at the same chronological age
Waaijer et al., 2016 — 178 adults aged 45–81, Leiden Longevity Study, sun-protected arm biopsies
What it means: Senescent-cell burden in human skin tracks visible ageing, even in skin that sees little sun.
What it does not mean: It does not show that senescent cells cause wrinkles, or that removing them would reverse any. One observational cohort shows an association.
units.sourceNote: Waaijer 2016 (Leiden Longevity Study) · Ressler 2006

units.text:
Four registers
Human, mouse or dish?
Senescence research mixes human tissue, mice and cultured cells. For the ageing dermis the four answers point in different directions, which is why they belong in separate sentences.
Mechanism
A collagen-fragmentation loop
Skin collagen falls with age. Aged human dermis shows more fibroblast MMP-1 and fragmented collagen; in culture, fragmentation raises MMP-1 further. That senescent cells drive this in living skin is plausible, not shown.
Human evidence
Association
p16-positive cells rise with age and track with wrinkles and perceived age
Animal evidence
Causation, in mice
Clearing p16-positive cells, or giving senolytic drugs, extends healthy lifespan in mice. Skin was checked only for safety, and clearing these cells during healing slowed wound closure.
Open question
Do senotherapies change human skin?

units.text:
Where the evidence is strongest
The levers with trials behind them.
Two ways of protecting or rebuilding the dermal matrix have randomized human trials. In a community trial of 903 adults, daily sunscreen for four and a half years slowed photoageing compared with discretionary use (GRADE B). Topical tretinoin improves photoageing consistently across randomized trials, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates topical retinoids first-line, GRADE A. Retinol improved fine wrinkles in very old skin in a small trial (C), and within a week it raised collagen synthesis and lowered MMPs in biopsies of aged human skin.
Daily sunscreen: one large RCT (B)

units.text:
Mechanism
The skin regenerates its own cortisol.
Skin expresses the machinery of a local stress axis, including CRH and POMC with its product ACTH. Keratinocytes and dermal fibroblasts also carry 11β-HSD1, the enzyme that turns inactive cortisone back into active cortisol inside the cell. In human skin samples its activity is higher with age and in sun-exposed skin, and local cortisol availability is set independently of blood levels. Cortisol slows collagen production in dermal fibroblasts, and mice lacking the enzyme kept their dermal thickness with age.
Local axis: CRH, POMC and ACTH are made in skin
11β-HSD1 regenerates cortisol inside skin cells
Mechanism register: human samples, cultured cells and mice

The evidence
Rare, and usually from a prescription.
Endogenous Cushing's syndrome is uncommon: European population studies put it at two to three new cases per million people a year. The commonest cause of Cushing's syndrome is iatrogenic, from glucocorticoids given as medicine. The Endocrine Society therefore asks for a drug history first, covering tablets, inhalers, injections and creams, including skin-bleaching products, and recommends testing when features are multiple and progressive.

What changes in practice
Reassure the many, refer the few.
When a patient asks about 'cortisol face', start with the drug history: steroid creams, skin-lighteners, herbal tonics and injections. Then look for the discriminating features. Without them, the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide reads most puffiness as sleep, alcohol, salt and fluid, and the Endocrine Society recommends against widespread testing. With them, especially when they are progressing, the next step is formal testing and an endocrinologist. A cortisol supplement or a consumer cortisol panel answers the wrong question.

Lesson 2.2 · Concept
Estrogen and the dermis.
Skin carries estrogen receptors (ERα, ERβ and the membrane receptor GPER) in both sun-protected and sun-damaged sites. In postmenopausal women, two weeks of topical estradiol raised collagen production in sun-protected hip skin; photoaged facial skin showed no such response. After menopause, small biopsy studies found skin collagen and thickness falling year by year, following years since menopause more closely than age. That is mechanism and natural history. What hormone therapy does to a face is a separate question.

Topical estradiol raises collagen in sun-protected skin only

The evidence
One to two per cent a year.
In small biopsy studies of postmenopausal women, skin collagen content and skin thickness fell by about 1–2% a year, in step with bone mass, and followed years since menopause more than age. Reviews, and the Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide, quote a steeper early loss of up to 30% in the first five years. That figure traces to the same small studies, and a check of their abstracts in September 2026 did not find it stated.

Human evidence
Biopsy gains, mirror results.
Hormone therapy has two kinds of trial behind it. Small trials measure the dermis; larger trials measure the face. They point in different directions, so read them separately. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide grades the skin benefit B; the North American Menopause Society rates the same evidence 'limited or inconsistent'. This course grades the structural gains C and teaches the negative wrinkle trials alongside them.

Regulatory status and indications
Symptoms and bone. Skin is a bystander.
In the US, as of February 2026, FDA-approved menopausal hormone therapy is for moderate-to-severe hot flashes, vaginal and vulvar symptoms and, for some products, preventing bone loss. FDA's 2025–26 labeling changes removed cardiovascular, breast-cancer and dementia statements from the boxed warning; skin did not become an indication. The North American Menopause Society's 2022 statement finds benefit outweighs risk for bothersome symptoms and bone protection when therapy starts before 60 or within 10 years of menopause, and finds insufficient evidence for compounded 'bioidentical' hormones. Under US rules an over-the-counter 'hormone cream' is an unapproved drug. For the skin itself, daily sunscreen has a large randomized trial behind it, and one tretinoin cream is FDA-approved as an adjunct for fine facial wrinkl…

units.text: In the UK, as of September 2026, HRT products such as estradiol patches and gel are prescription-only medicines licensed for oestrogen-deficiency symptoms and, for some, for preventing osteoporosis in women at high risk of fracture; skin is not among their uses. A compounded 'bioidentical' hormone is an unlicensed medicine in the UK, and MHRA guidance puts a licensed product first when one can meet the need. On the UK medicines compendium, topical tretinoin appears only in acne treatments.

In the EU, the harmonised core product information for HRT (CMDh, December 2025) lists oestrogen-deficiency symptoms after menopause, osteoporosis prevention and vaginal atrophy as its indications; skin is not an indication. EU cosmetics law prohibits oestrogens, progestogens and tretinoin in cosmetic products (Regulation (EC) No 1223/2009, Annex II), and anti-wrinkle products containing tretinoin marketed as cosmetics are illegal cosmetics.

In Portugal, as of September 2026, the estradiol HRT products Estreva gel and Estrofem tablets are authorised for symptoms of oestrogen deficiency in postmenopausal women. The topical tretinoin product Ketrel cream is authorised and prescription-only on INFARMED's database, with indications for acne (except acne rosacea) and keratinisation disorders.

In Brazil, as of September 2026, estradiol for menopausal hormone therapy is registered and the Oestrogel label covers menopausal symptoms and prevention of postmenopausal osteoporosis, not skin ageing, while the Vitacid label for topical tretinoin names cutaneous photoageing as well as acne vulgaris. The Federal Council of Medicine (CFM) bars physicians from using hormones, in any formulation, except in diagnosed deficiencies where replacement shows evidence of scientifically proven benefit (Resolution 1.999/2012), and from prescribing hormones marketed as 'bioidentical' or 'nano' without proof of superiority (Resolution 2.333/2023).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE), the federal regulator of medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, registers estradiol products as Prescription Only Medicines, for example Oestrogel gel (since 11 November 2021). The EDE register lists therapeutic categories rather than indications, so it does not show whether any UAE label includes a skin indication (25 September 2026). Under the medicines law, Federal Decree-Law 38 of 2024, a compounding pharmacy may not compound products that are essentially copies of EDE-approved products unless no commercially available product can deliver the expected benefit to the patient.

Lesson 2.3 · Concept
Some syndromes show on the skin first.
A handful of inherited endocrine syndromes appear on the skin before the glands declare themselves. In multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1), multiple facial angiofibromas and collagenomas are common. In Carney complex, lentigines on the lips, eyelids and canthi, blue naevi and small skin myxomas sit alongside myxomas of the heart and cortisol-secreting adrenal disease. In MEN2A, an itchy, rippled, pigmented plaque between the shoulder blades can precede medullary thyroid cancer.
MEN1: facial angiofibromas, collagenomas
Carney complex: lip and eyelid lentigines, myxomas
MEN2A: lichen amyloidosis between the shoulder blades

units.text:
The evidence
Eighty-eight per cent.
In a consecutive series of 32 people with MEN1 examined at the US National Institutes of Health, 88% had multiple facial angiofibromas and 72% had collagenomas. The angiofibromas were clinically and histologically identical to those of tuberous sclerosis. The authors concluded that angiofibromas in someone without tuberous sclerosis call for biochemical testing for MEN1.
of 32 people with MEN1 had multiple facial angiofibromas
Darling et al., 1997 — collagenomas in 72%
What it means: Multiple facial angiofibromas are common in MEN1 and can be its first visible sign; in someone without tuberous sclerosis they are a reason for endocrine testing, whatever the cosmetic plan.
What it does not mean: It does not mean a single facial papule is MEN1. This is one small referral-centre series, and angiofibromas have other causes, tuberous sclerosis above all.

units.text:
Concept
The everyday endocrine signs.
Most endocrine skin signs you meet come from common disease. New generalised darkening, strongest in skin creases, scars, mucosa and sun-exposed skin, can signal primary adrenal insufficiency, which can turn into a life-threatening crisis. Hirsutism that appears fast, keeps progressing, or comes with a deepening voice or clitoromegaly makes an androgen-secreting tumour more likely. Velvety dark plaques of acanthosis nigricans track insulin resistance, pretibial myxoedema points to Graves' disease, and cold, dry skin suggests hypothyroidism.
Darkening in creases, scars and gums: adrenal insufficiency
Rapid hirsutism or virilization: exclude a tumour
Acanthosis, pretibial plaques, dry cool skin: metabolic and thyroid

Module 03 · Fat, incretins and the ageing face
The face changes when the fat does.

units.text:
Mechanism
The skin keeps its own fat.
Beneath the dermis lies subcutaneous fat. Within the reticular dermis itself sits a thinner layer, dermal white adipose tissue. In mice, this layer expands rapidly after a Staphylococcus aureus infection, its new fat cells release the antimicrobial peptide cathelicidin, and the capacity fades with age through TGF-β signalling. Human skin arranges this fat differently, in cones around hair follicles, and human acne lesions contain perifollicular preadipocytes that make cathelicidin. What the layer contributes to human skin ageing has not been measured.
A second fat layer inside the dermis
In mice: antimicrobial, and lost with age
In people: a different shape, and an open question about ageing

Human evidence
Fat that holds the face up.
Cadaver dissection shows that the face's subcutaneous fat sits in separate compartments, and facial ageing is partly how each compartment changes. Weight shows the same thing from the outside. In a study of 186 pairs of identical twins, the twin with the higher body-mass index looked older before about age 40 and younger after it.
pairs of identical twins compared for facial ageing
Guyuron et al., 2009 — a four-point higher BMI tracked with an older look before about 40 and a younger look after it
What it means: From midlife on, facial fat goes with a younger-looking face. That fits the anatomy: the face ages partly as its fat compartments change. GRADE C, observational.
What it does not mean: It is an observational comparison of photographs. It does not show that gaining weight rejuvenates, or that fat loss on a drug changes the skin itself.

units.text:
Mechanism
Sugar that sticks to collagen.
Glycation is a slow, non-enzymatic reaction. Reducing sugars attach to protein amino groups, rearrange into Amadori products and end as advanced glycation end products, or AGEs. On long-lived dermal collagen, AGEs form cross-links that stiffen the matrix. Through their receptor, RAGE, AGEs switch on inflammatory signalling in laboratory studies. The Aesthetic & Regenerative Endocrinology guide rates the structural and inflammatory effects B; the course grades the causal link to visible ageing D, because the human data are associations.
Sugar + protein → Schiff base → Amadori product → AGE
Cross-links stiffen long-lived collagen
RAGE signalling: shown in the laboratory

Human evidence
Fifteen years on the same collagen.
Human skin collagen turns over slowly; tissue analysis puts its half-life at about 15 years. In skin biopsies, glycoxidation products in collagen rose about five-fold between ages 20 and 85, and were up to twice as high in type 1 diabetes. Skin autofluorescence, a non-invasive reading, correlates moderately with those biopsy measures and was validated in non-pigmented skin.

Lesson 3.2 · Concept
Two gut hormones, re-engineered.
GLP-1 and GIP are incretins, hormones the gut releases after a meal that amplify glucose-dependent insulin release; GLP-1 also slows gastric emptying and reduces appetite. Native GLP-1 is broken down within minutes. Semaglutide is a long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist, and tirzepatide activates both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. In the US, as of September 2026, both are FDA-approved drugs for defined indications, set out in the next moment.

Semaglutide: GLP-1 receptor agonist
Tirzepatide: GIP and GLP-1 receptor agonist

units.text: In the UK both are licensed by the MHRA, and tirzepatide's diabetes and weight-management uses share one brand, Mounjaro.

In the EU, semaglutide is a centrally authorised prescription medicine, as Ozempic and Rybelsus for diabetes and Wegovy for weight management (EMA and HMA, June 2024), and tirzepatide is authorised as Mounjaro (EU-wide, 15 September 2022) for diabetes and adult weight management, prescription-only. A search of the Union Register and EMA's medicines data on 25 September 2026 found no EU product named Zepbound.

In Brazil, ANVISA has registered semaglutide as Ozempic (since 6 August 2018) and Wegovy (since 2 January 2023), with synthetic semaglutide pens registered from 26 May 2026, and tirzepatide as Mounjaro (since 25 September 2023); a search of its register on 25 September 2026 found no product named Zepbound. Since 23 June 2025, GLP-1 receptor agonist medicines may only be sold with retention of the prescription (RDC 973/2025 and IN 360/2025).

In the UAE, the Emirates Drug Establishment (EDE) has been the federal authority regulating medical products since Federal Decree-Law 28/2023, and its register lists semaglutide as Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy and tirzepatide as Mounjaro; every entry checked is a Prescription Only Medicine. A search of the EDE register on 25 September 2026 found no product named Zepbound.
